title: Custom Hooks
subtitle: Extracting and reusing stateful logic with custom hooks
author: KERNAL Team

whyItExists.problem: The same stateful logic pattern appears in multiple components — fetch data from an API, sync a value to localStorage, debounce an input. Copy-pasting useState + useEffect between components violates DRY and is hard to maintain.
whyItExists.solution: Custom hooks are plain JavaScript functions whose names start with 'use' and that call other hooks inside. They let you extract stateful logic into a reusable function that can be shared across components.
whyItExists.whenToUse: When the same useState + useEffect combination appears in two or more components. When a component is doing too much because of repeated boilerplate. When you want to test state logic independently.
whyItExists.whenNotToUse: Don't extract a hook that would be used only once — it's premature abstraction. The hook should encapsulate logic, not just rename useState.

explainModes.beginner: A custom hook is just a function that starts with 'use' and uses React hooks inside. You call it from a component exactly like useState or useEffect. The magic is that each component that calls your hook gets its own independent state — hooks are not shared between components.
explainModes.simple: Name must start with use (enforced by the linter). Can call any other hooks inside. Returns whatever the caller needs (values, setters, actions). Each component that uses the hook gets its own state instance — not shared. Extract: useWindowSize(), useFetch(url), useLocalStorage(key, initial), useDebounce(value, ms), useToggle(initial).
explainModes.standard: The rules of hooks apply to custom hooks too: no conditionals, no loops. Custom hooks don't need to return JSX — they're about logic, not UI. A custom hook can use other custom hooks. Testing: test the hook in isolation with renderHook from @testing-library/react. Sharing hooks: publish as an npm package or use a hooks library like react-use.
explainModes.technical: Each call to a custom hook creates an independent closure — two components calling useCounter() have independent counts. The hook's internal useState calls are stored in the component's fiber (not in the hook function itself). This is why you can call the same hook multiple times in one component and each call is independent. Type-safe hooks in TypeScript: function useFetch<T>(url: string): { data: T | null, loading: boolean, error: string | null }.
explainModes.deepDive: Composition: combine custom hooks: useFetch uses useEffect, useRef (for the ignore flag), and useState. usePaginatedFetch uses useFetch + useState for the page number. Hook libraries: react-use (100+ hooks), @tanstack/react-query (server state + caching), swr (stale-while-revalidate). These are custom hooks refined into production-quality libraries. The ecosystem: React's hooks model makes it easy to share logic as hooks — any npm package that exports a useX function is usable directly in your components.

questions.question: Two components both call `useCounter()`. Do they share the same counter state?
options: Yes — custom hooks share state between all components that call them
No — each component that calls a custom hook gets its own independent state instance
It depends on whether the hook uses useState or useRef internally
Yes, unless you wrap the hook in React.memo
questions.explanation: Custom hooks do NOT share state — they share LOGIC. When two components each call useCounter(), React creates independent useState calls for each component instance. The hook function runs once per component per render, producing independent state. To share state between components, you need Context or an external store.

faq.q: Why must custom hook names start with 'use'?
faq.a: This is enforced by the react-hooks ESLint plugin. It's how React (and the linter) knows to apply the rules of hooks to your function: no conditional calls, always called in the same order. A function named 'fetchData' (without 'use') won't be checked — you could accidentally call it conditionally and violate hook rules silently.
